series: LMArena (Chatbot Arena) top text score, monthly, May 2023 to Oct 2026
unit: Arena score (Elo-scale, Bradley-Terry since Dec 2023/Jan 2024); relative between models, no human reference line
description: People-graded series. Main points: the #1 model's Arena score on the text leaderboard (non style-controlled, overall category) in the last published snapshot of each month, plus the first snapshot with proprietary models (May 8, 2023). Each point also carries the score of a fixed anchor model in the same snapshot (GPT-4 March 2023: "gpt-4-0314", or the single "gpt-4" entry before Dec 2023) and the implied probability that a voter prefers the top model over that anchor, 1 / (1 + 10^(-gap/400)). The gap is the more comparable quantity across time, because the raw score's offset moves when the model pool or methodology changes. other_series: creative-writing category top; style-controlled top; GDPval and Remote Labor Index (expert human graders with a human-professional reference); and dated human-vs-model writing studies.
license: LMArena leaderboard-dataset: CC BY 4.0. LMArena HF space snapshot files: published by LMArena (lmsys) in a public Hugging Face space with no license field; cited, values only. Epoch AI (GDPval, RLI copies): CC BY 4.0. Studies: cited for single published numbers.
no_human_reference: Arena scores are relative between models: they say which model voters preferred, not how either compares with a human writer. There is no human line on this chart and none can be drawn from this data. The anchored win probability is still model vs model (top model vs GPT-4 of March 2023).
sources: https://huggingface.co/spaces/lmarena-ai/arena-leaderboard (formerly lmarena-ai/chatbot-arena-leaderboard and lmsys/chatbot-arena-leaderboard), revision 6f2eeeba09bf42144dbc118fe1a8e12e4c533f9d: elo_results_YYYYMMDD.pkl (2023-05-08 to 2025-08-29) and leaderboard_table_YYYYMMDD.csv (2023 cross-check)
caveats: Elo is relative: no human reference line. A rising top score means voters increasingly prefer the newest model to the rest of the pool; it does not measure distance to, or past, human writers.

The raw score is not a fixed scale. Methodology changed: online Elo to Bradley-Terry (Dec 2023/Jan 9, 2024), style control as the default (May 16, 2025), frequency re-weighting (July 23, 2025), plus a growing and changing model pool. The anchor model gpt-4-0314 sat at about 1186 from 2024 to Apr 2025, then about 1204 to 1212, so part of the mid-2025 raw rise is scale. Use gap_vs_anchor or implied_win_prob_vs_anchor for trends.

LMArena's official leaderboard-dataset omits models later deprecated or renamed (Claude 1/2, Bard, gemini-exp-*, gemini-1.5-pro-exp-*, gemini-2.5-pro-exp-03-25, early-grok-3 and others) and its 2023 rows are missing all proprietary models. In every month-end snapshot from Oct 2024 to May 2025 the dataset is missing the #1 model (its top is understated by 5 to 41 points), and from May 2023 to Jan 2024 it is missing the top model in every month (by 60 to 180 points). On 2024-05-27 the dataset and the snapshot file also disagree by 5.5 points for the same model. This file therefore uses the snapshot files LMArena published at the time (through Aug 29, 2025) and the dataset only after that. For Sept 2025 on, the dataset matched archived copies of the public leaderboard on Dec 16, 2025, Mar 11, 2026 and Sept 13, 2026 (same top models and scores, style-controlled view).

Voters are self-selected arena users with their own prompts; style (length, formatting, markdown) sways votes, which is why style control exists. Labs have tested many private variants before release (Singh et al., "The Leaderboard Illusion", arXiv 2504.20879, Apr 2025), so the public top is a selected maximum.
Monthly points are the last snapshot of the month; LMArena publishes irregularly (several times a month in 2024 to 2026, about monthly in 2023). The Oct 2026 point is Oct 15.

Writing studies: different genres, raters, lengths and metrics; do not draw one line through them. Lay vs expert raters is the largest moderator (experts reject prompted AI fiction; lay readers often prefer it). Labels alone move ratings. Short excerpts favor AI; longer works and translations favor humans. Publication dates lag data collection by up to 2.5 years (model_or_data_date where known).

GDPval figures come from OpenAI's GDPval (graded by industry experts) via Epoch's copy; OpenAI built the benchmark and ranks its own models, a conflict of interest. RLI (Scale AI and the Center for AI Safety) uses trained human evaluators. Both have a meaningful human reference (50% parity for GDPval, 100% for RLI) unlike the arena.
LLM-judged writing leaderboards (e.g. Lech Mazur's, in Epoch's hub as lech_mazur_writing_external.csv) are excluded on purpose: the grader is a model, not a person.

other_series.unit: varies by study; see metric_kind, definition and reference_line
other_series.description: One point per study, dated by publication (or arXiv v1). metric_kind: identification_accuracy (chance 50), judged_human_rate (50 = indistinguishable in three-party designs), preference_share_for_ai or _for_human (parity 50), rating_ai_vs_human (compare value with human_value), persuasion (0 = no difference), assisted_vs_unassisted, detection_by_experts.

points.note: Jakesch, Hancock and Naaman, PNAS. Pre-ChatGPT models.
points.definition: % of optimized AI self-presentations judged human (real human texts: 51.7%); overall detection accuracy 50 to 52%
points.human_group: real dating, professional and hospitality profiles

points.note: Ayers et al., JAMA Internal Medicine. Adjacent genre (medical advice); chatbot answers were about 4x longer.
points.definition: % of evaluations preferring the chatbot answer over a physician's (95% CI 75.0 to 81.8)

points.note: "Human or Not?" two-minute gamified Turing test.
points.definition: % correct when the chat partner was an AI (68% overall); chance 50

points.note: Spitale, Biller-Andorno and Germani, Science Advances.
points.definition: % of GPT-3 tweets correctly recognized as AI (organic tweets recognized as human: 63%)

points.note: Chakrabarty et al., "Art or Artifice", CHI 2024 (arXiv v1 date). Expert raters; large human advantage.
points.definition: mean % of the 14 Torrance Test of Creative Writing checks passed (best model Claude v1.3; GPT-4 27.9, GPT-3.5 8.7) vs New Yorker stories 84.7

points.note: Gomez-Rodriguez and Williams, "A Confederacy of Models", Findings of EMNLP 2023. Humans slightly ahead on creativity and dark humor (n.s.).
points.definition: mean rubric total out of 100 for GPT-4 vs human writers 70.1

points.note: Herbold et al., Scientific Reports. Two model generations in one protocol.
points.definition: mean teacher rating (0 to 6) for GPT-4 essays; ChatGPT-3.5 4.36; student essays 3.69

points.note: Jones and Bergen, two-party Turing test; not comparable with the 2025 three-party design.
points.definition: % of two-party games in which the witness was judged human (real humans 67, GPT-3.5 50, ELIZA 22)

points.note: Scarfe et al., PLOS ONE. AI did worse on the final-year module.
points.definition: probability that a set of AI exam submissions outgrades a random same-size set of real students' (94% of AI submissions went undetected)

points.note: Marco, Gonzalo et al., "Pron vs Prompt", EMNLP 2024. Expert raters; large human advantage.
points.definition: mean style-originality score (0 to 3) for GPT-4 in English vs Patricio Pron 1.70

points.note: Doshi and Hauser, Science Advances. Not AI text vs human text: AI-assisted vs unassisted human writing.
points.definition: % increase in evaluator-rated story novelty for writers given AI ideas vs human-only writers (usefulness +9.0%); stories became more similar to each other

points.note: Marco, Rello and Gonzalo, COLING 2025. Small fine-tuned model, very short texts.
points.definition: mean reader rating for a fine-tuned BART-large vs average human writers 1.85
points.human_group: human writers of short movie synopses

points.note: Porter and Machery, Scientific Reports 14:26133. Study 2: AI poems rated higher overall (d = 0.67), most on rhythm; 89% of AI poems rhymed every line vs 40% of human poems; authors attribute the preference to AI poems being simpler and more accessible. Being told a poem was AI lowered ratings.
points.definition: % correct when judging each poem AI or human (below chance 50); AI poems were judged human more often than real poems
points.human_group: ten canonical English poets (Shakespeare, Byron, Dickinson, Eliot and others)
points.raters: lay (90% read poetry a few times a year or less)

points.model: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o1-Pro (incl. humanizer evasion)
points.note: Russell, Karpinska and Iyyer, ACL 2025. Counterpoint: practiced readers detect AI text.
points.definition: % accuracy of a majority vote of 5 frequent-LLM-user annotators on AI vs human articles; nonexperts near chance

points.note: Jones and Bergen. The persona prompt is decisive; five-minute chats.
points.definition: % of three-party games in which persona-prompted GPT-4.5 was picked as the human over a real human; without the persona 36%

points.note: Salvi et al., Nature Human Behaviour. Non-personalized GPT-4 not significantly better than humans.
points.definition: % of non-tied debates in which personalized GPT-4 was more persuasive than a human opponent

points.note: Bai et al., Nature Communications. Fielded Nov to Dec 2022.
points.definition: difference in policy support (0 to 100 scale), AI message minus lay-human message, Study 1 (Study 2: -0.52); both not significant

points.note: Haverals and Martin, "The human-authorship halo" (v2 title). Labels move preference.
